analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal capital gains tax for individuals and corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in March 1997, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received any further action, hearing, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal tax on capital gains — the profits from selling stocks, businesses, real estate, and other investments held over a year — for individuals and corporations alike. It would have done this by making the entire net capital gain a deduction from taxable income [S2][S3]. For most households, wages and salaries are the main income and remain fully taxed; investment profit is concentrated among the wealthiest households, so a full repeal primarily cuts taxes for those at the top. The bill was never taken up by the committee it was sent to and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations with large realized investment gains. Capital gains are heavily concentrated among the wealthiest Americans and among corporations selling assets, so the largest dollar savings would go to those groups. Investors in mutual funds, partnerships, REITs, and S corporations would benefit through special rules the bill sets up for those entities [S3]. Anyone selling an appreciated asset — including a small business owner or a home seller with a large profit — would owe no federal tax on the gain [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces the existing capital gains tax structure with a rule that 100 percent of a taxpayer's net capital gain is a deduction from gross income, meaning no tax is owed on it [S2][S3].

It applies to both individuals and corporations, repealing the corporate alternative capital gains tax provisions and the special small-business stock exclusion (Section 1202), which would no longer be needed [S2][S3].

The bill includes transitional rules and coordinated treatment for pass-through entities — regulated investment companies (mutual funds), REITs, S corporations, partnerships, estates, trusts, and common trust funds — so gains flowing through those vehicles would also be untaxed at the owner level [S3].
It would apply to tax years ending after December 31, 1996, with special transition rules for the 1997 taxable year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers overall. Capital gains taxation is a source of federal revenue; eliminating it means that revenue must be replaced by other taxes, borrowed, or offset by spending cuts. Since the tax cut is proportional to investment gains, the largest dollar benefits go to those with the largest gains, while the cost of replacing the revenue falls on the general taxpayer base. Workers whose income is wages would receive no benefit from the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and the federal treasury

drawbacks.text: The benefits are heavily tilted toward high-income households: capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthiest taxpayers and corporations, so a full repeal would deliver the largest tax cuts to them while ordinary wage earners get little or nothing.

Eliminating the capital gains tax removes federal revenue. Because the bill contains no replacement revenue, the lost money would have to come from higher taxes elsewhere, larger deficits, or spending cuts, the costs of which fall broadly on taxpayers and users of government services.

The bill favors investors relative to workers: by untaxing profits from asset sales entirely while leaving wages and salaries fully taxed, it changes the effective tax mix in a way that advantages income from owning assets over income from working.

The bill's own transition and coordination rules (for example, reducing the deduction by investment income taken into account under the investment-interest limitation, and special rules for trusts and estates) would add complexity to the tax code even while simplifying the capital gains rate structure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real for anyone selling appreciated assets: no federal tax on the profit. But that benefit is distributed by how much capital gain you realize, which means the top of the income and wealth distribution gets the overwhelming share of the money. The cost — lost federal revenue that must be made up somewhere — is spread across all taxpayers and future taxpayers. An honest weighing: this is a large tax cut aimed at a narrow, asset-owning slice of the population, paid for by everyone, with no offsetting provisions for low- or middle-income households. The case supporters would make is that taxing gains discourages investment and locks sellers into assets; the full-repeal approach goes far beyond the more moderate targeted rate cuts Congress actually enacted in 1997.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 1997, and the committee never considered it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane, joined by Rep. J.D. Hayworth, introduced the bill on March 19, 1997 [S1][S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
Ten Republican members cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the federal government kept collecting capital gains revenue that would otherwise have been lost, and no windfall tax cut flowed to the households and corporations with the largest investment gains. Ordinary taxpayers were spared the shifted cost of replacing that revenue.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; all 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill never moved beyond referral.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate all federal tax on investment gains, with the largest dollar savings flowing to those who realize the largest gains — concentrated among the wealthiest households. The cost of the lost revenue falls on the general taxpayer base.

The bill includes special rules for mutual funds, REITs, and other investment vehicles so gains passed through to shareholders would also go untaxed. Untaxed gains could increase trading and asset sales, activity that generates fees for the industry.

Sales of appreciated real estate held more than a year would become fully tax-free, a large benefit to investors and developers. Ordinary home sellers would also benefit, though most already receive substantial exclusions on home-sale gains.

The bill repeals the corporate capital gains tax provisions, so corporations selling capital assets would owe no tax on the gains. The revenue foregone would otherwise be part of the general tax base paid by businesses and individuals.
